I have mentioned that he was a poet. At the age of three-and-twenty he published his first poem, which the entire nation greeted with rapture and enthusiasm. His fortunate star never ceased to shine; no reputation had ever risen with such swiftness, or spread so universally. The crowd praised the very verses that astonished the philosopher in his study; not a single voice dissented.

At this moment, in the full splendour of his fame, he first met Elinor. She was a young heiress of rare beauty, living in the charge of her guardian. From their earliest appearance together, they seemed made for one another. Elinor did not possess Woodville’s genius, but her spirit was noble and generous; her youth, and the affection she inspired wherever she went, raised her above acquaintance with anything save goodness and excellence. She was beautiful, her manner open and unaffected, and her deep blue eyes shone with that radiance which feeling united to wisdom alone can bestow.

Created for each other, they quickly fell in love. Woodville knew love’s delight for the first time, while Elinor rejoiced in owning the heart of one so lovely and so distinguished among his fellow men. What could such a union promise but joy without alloy?

Woodville was a Poet: every circle sought his presence, and wherever he appeared every gaze rested upon him alone. Yet he was a poor clergyman’s son, while Elinor possessed a rich inheritance. Her guardian looked favourably upon their attachment. Woodville’s merits were too conspicuous to permit objection to his smaller fortune. Her father’s final will, however, forbade her to marry before attaining her majority, and retaining her wealth depended upon obedience to this command. She had only just entered her twentieth year, and the lovers had to accept the postponement. Yet they were always in each other’s company, and their happiness appeared paradisal. They studied side by side and planned their future pursuits; drawing love and gladness from each other’s words and looks, they scarcely lamented the delay of their complete union. Woodville’s renown rose ever higher, and Elinor grew in wisdom and loveliness under her accomplished lover’s instruction.

Only two months remained before Elinor would be twenty-one, and every preparation for their marriage was complete. How can I tell of the disaster that ended such felicity? Yet this earth, overgrown with sorrow and decay, would not be the earth we know had these two angelic beings been allowed to live for one another. Search the whole world: nowhere will you discover the perfect happiness their marriage would have afforded them. The established order among us wretched inhabitants of earth must have been overturned to permit such consummate bliss.

“But it is remarkable that she always hears Jane more easily than she hears me. Jane speaks so clearly! Still, she won’t find her grandmother any deafer than she was two years ago, which is quite something at my mother’s age. And it really has been a full two years since she was here, you know. We’ve never gone so long without seeing her, and as I told Mrs. Cole, we’ll hardly know how to make enough fuss over her now.”

“Are you expecting Miss Fairfax to visit soon?”

“Oh yes, next week.”

“Really! That must be a wonderful pleasure.”

“Thank you. How kind you are. Yes, next week. Everyone is so surprised, and everyone says the same lovely things. I’m sure she’ll be every bit as happy to see her friends in Highbury as they’ll be to see her. Yes, Friday or Saturday; she can’t say which, because Colonel Campbell needs the carriage himself on one of those days. It’s so good of them to send her all the way! But they always do, you know. Oh yes, next Friday or Saturday. That’s what her letter is about. That’s why she has written outside the schedule, as we call it; ordinarily we wouldn’t have heard from her until next Tuesday or Wednesday.”

“Yes, that’s what I thought. I was afraid there was little chance of hearing anything about Miss Fairfax today.”

“How kind of you! No, we wouldn’t have heard, except for this special circumstance, her coming here so soon. My mother is delighted! She’s going to stay at least three months. Three months—she says so quite definitely, as I shall have the pleasure of reading to you. You see, the Campbells are going to Ireland. Mrs. Dixon has persuaded her parents to come and see her at once. They hadn’t planned to go until summer, but she’s so impatient to see them again. Before she married last October, she had never spent even a week away from them, which must make it very strange to be in different kingdoms, I was going to say, but different countries, anyway. So she wrote a very urgent letter to her mother—or her father; honestly, I can’t remember which, but we’ll find out in a moment from Jane’s letter. She wrote for Mr. Dixon as well as herself, asking them to come immediately. They would meet them in Dublin and take them back to their country home, Baly-craig, a beautiful place, I imagine.”

“What conclusion have you reached, then? What picture have I put in your mind?”

Dupin’s question made my skin crawl. “A madman did it,” I said. “Some raving lunatic who escaped from a nearby asylum.”

“Your idea is relevant in some ways,” he answered. “But even at their most frantic, madmen do not make sounds like that strange voice heard on the stairs. They come from some country, and however confused their words, their speech still consists of recognizable syllables. Besides, a madman’s hair does not look like this.” He held out a small tuft. “I removed it from Madame L’Espanaye’s tightly clenched fingers. Tell me what you think.”

“Dupin!” I cried, thoroughly shaken. “This hair is extraordinary. It isn’t human hair.”

“I haven’t said it was,” he replied. “But before we settle that, look at this small drawing I have made. It is an exact copy of the marks on Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s throat. One witness described them as dark bruises and deep nail marks. Dumas and Etienne described a series of dark spots that were clearly finger impressions.

“As you can see,” my friend continued, laying the paper on the table in front of us, “the drawing suggests a firm grip that never shifted. Nothing seems to have slipped. Each finger kept its terrible hold where it first dug in, perhaps until the victim died. Now try putting all your fingers into the corresponding marks at once.”

I tried, but could not do it.

“Perhaps this is not a fair test,” he said. “The paper lies flat, whereas a human throat is round. Here is a piece of wood about the same size around as a throat. Wrap the drawing around it and try again.”

I followed his directions, but the problem was even clearer this time. “No human hand made these marks,” I said.

“Now read this passage from Cuvier,” Dupin replied.

It was a detailed account of the anatomy and general features of the large, reddish-brown orangutan of the East Indian Islands. Everyone knows something of these animals’ enormous size, tremendous strength and agility, fierce temper, and tendency to imitate what they see. All the horror of the murder became clear to me at once.

“The description of its fingers,” I said when I had finished reading, “matches this drawing exactly.”
